breakfast.name: Suutei Tsai (Milk Tea)
instructions: Boil water, add tea
Add milk and salt
Simmer, add butter
Strain and serve
breakfast.description: Salty butter milk tea — the Mongolian day starts with this.

breakfast.name: Aaruul (Dried Curd)
instructions: Strain curd
Shape into small pieces
Dry in sun for several days
Store and eat as hard snack
breakfast.description: Hard dried curd pieces — traditional nomad food.

breakfast.name: Tsuivan (Fried Noodles with Meat)
instructions: Tsuivan noodles are made by hand: mix flour, water, salt into a stiff dough
Roll very thin, cut into strips, steam briefly
The steaming pre-cooks the noodles
Fry mutton with onion and carrot in fat
Add steamed noodles — toss and fry together
The noodles absorb the mutton fat and brown slightly
Season with salt and pepper
No other spices — Mongolian food is genuinely minimally spiced
Tsuivan is Mongolia's most popular everyday dish
The hand-stretched noodles are central — the texture is specific to this technique
Mongolian cooking reflects the pastoral nomadic tradition: simple, hearty, meat-central
breakfast.description: Mongolia's most popular everyday dish — hand-stretched noodles steamed then stir-fried with mutton, onion, and carrot. The minimal spicing (salt, pepper only) reflects the nomadic pastoral tradition: the mutton fat is the flavor. Hand-stretching gives a specific chewy texture that machine-cut noodles don't replicate.

breakfast.name: Süütei Tsai (Milk Tea)
ingredients: Pu-erh or brick tea (the Mongolian tea)
Salt (small amount — Mongolian tea is salted, not sweetened)
instructions: Boil water
Add brick tea — simmer 5 minutes
Add milk — roughly equal water and milk
Add salt — the salt is not optional; Mongolian tea is always salty
Simmer together briefly
Optional: add a small amount of animal fat (tallow or butter)
Optional: whisk in a spoon of flour for a thicker 'soup' version
Süütei tsai is not a drink so much as a food — it provides calories and hydration together
Drunk throughout the day — offered to every visitor as the first gesture
Refusing süütei tsai in a Mongolian ger (yurt) is impolite
The salty, milky tea is divisive for outsiders — deeply comforting for Mongolians
The salt in tea tradition is shared: Tibet (po cha), Kazakhstan, Central Asia
breakfast.description: Mongolia's salted milk tea — brick tea simmered with milk and salt, drunk throughout the day and offered to every visitor. The first hospitality gesture in any Mongolian ger (yurt). Salty, not sweet — the salt is cultural identity, not accident. The salted-milk-tea tradition is shared across Central Asia and Tibet. It provides calories and hydration simultaneously: food and drink in one.

lunch.name: Buuz (Steamed Dumplings)
ingredients: Filling: minced mutton, onion, garlic, salt, pepper
instructions: Make dough, rest
Mix mutton filling
Roll wrappers, fill generously
Pleat and pinch closed leaving small hole
Steam 20 min
lunch.description: Mongolia's national dish — steamed mutton dumplings.

lunch.name: Khuushuur (Fried Dumplings)
instructions: Make dough, roll circles
Fill with mutton mixture
Fold half-moon, seal
Deep fry until golden

lunch.name: Khorkhog (Stone Pressure Lamb)
instructions: Khorkhog is Mongolia's most iconic cooking method — pressure cooking with hot stones
Heat smooth river stones in a fire until extremely hot — white-hot
Fill a sealed metal container (milk churn or dedicated pot) with lamb pieces, vegetables, salt, water
Add the red-hot stones among the meat — use tongs, they're dangerous
Seal the container immediately — the stones generate extreme steam pressure inside
The pressure cooks the lamb in 30-45 minutes
The lamb is cooked by the radiant heat from the stones and the steam pressure
The meat is extraordinarily tender and has a unique smoky mineral flavor from the stones
Khorkhog is served at celebrations and as a way to cook in the open steppe — no oven needed
The stones are sometimes passed around after cooking — the fat on the stone is considered lucky
One of the world's most distinctive cooking techniques
lunch.description: Mongolia's hot-stone pressure cooking — bone-in lamb packed in a sealed container with vegetables and incandescent river stones, the stones generating intense steam pressure that cooks the lamb in 30-45 minutes. The mineral heat from stones gives a unique smoky flavor. One of the world's most distinctive cooking techniques: no oven, no equipment except stones and fire.

lunch.name: Chanasan Makh (Boiled Meat)
instructions: Place mutton in cold water — start cold to extract maximum flavor
Bring to boil, skim foam carefully — this is important for clarity
After skimming, the broth should be relatively clear
Add minimal salt — the meat flavor is the point
Simmer until the meat is cooked through — 45-60 minutes
Serve meat by slicing at the table
Broth drunk separately from a bowl
Mongolian approach to meat: boiling is the most respectful method
The meat's natural flavor should not be overwhelmed by spice
This is food that reflects the nomadic philosophy: the animal gives everything; cooking should not interfere with its quality
The quality of the mutton is entirely the dish — Mongolian steppe mutton is lean and flavorful
lunch.description: Mongolia's respect-for-meat cooking — mutton boiled with minimal seasoning to let the animal's natural flavor speak. The nomadic philosophy: the steppe animal gives everything; cooking should not obscure its quality. Mongolian steppe mutton is lean and distinctively flavored from grazing wild plants. The broth is drunk from a bowl; the meat is sliced at the table.

dinner.name: Khorkhog (Stone-Cooked Meat)
instructions: Heat river stones in fire until very hot
Layer meat, vegetables, and hot stones in metal pot
Add water, seal tightly
Cook 45-60 min
Open carefully — eat with hands
dinner.description: Lamb and vegetables cooked by hot stones inside a sealed pot.

dinner.name: Tsuivan (Fried Noodles)
instructions: Make noodles, cut into strips
Stir-fry mutton, add vegetables
Steam noodles on top of meat and vegetables
Toss together
dinner.description: Stir-fried noodles steamed over meat and vegetables.

dinner.name: Guriltai Shul (Noodle Soup)
instructions: The simplest Mongolian soup — noodles in mutton broth
Make or use pre-made noodles
Simmer mutton with water to make a simple stock
Add noodles — they cook in the broth
Add onion, carrot if using
Season with salt and pepper
Guriltai shul is the Mongolian school and home everyday soup
Every Mongolian child knows this soup
The broth from boiling mutton is the entire flavor — no other additions
The noodle-broth-mutton combination needs nothing else in the nomadic tradition
Eaten as a meal: the broth provides warmth and calories; the noodles provide starch; the meat provides protein
dinner.description: Mongolia's childhood soup — homemade noodles in mutton broth with minimal seasoning. Every Mongolian child grew up eating this. The mutton broth from simmered bones is the entire flavor foundation; no aromatics are required in the nomadic tradition. Noodles + mutton broth + meat: complete nutrition in its simplest form.

dinner.name: Boodog (Whole Marmot or Goat)
ingredients: Whole marmot (traditional, seasonal) or whole young goat
Hot stones (river stones heated in fire)
instructions: Boodog is Mongolia's most dramatic cooking technique — cooking from the inside out
Remove the entrails from a marmot or young goat
Keep the skin intact — it becomes the cooking vessel
Fill the cavity with hot stones and salt
Seal the opening — the stones cook from inside while the exterior is blowtorched
Both inside (from stones) and outside (from blowtorch or fire) are cooked simultaneously
The marmot skin is burned off with a blowtorch — the meat inside is cooked by steam from the stones
The result: steam-pressure-cooked meat from within, charred exterior
This is one of the most ancient cooking techniques in existence — cave-cooking principle
Marmot boodog is a Mongolian summer tradition — seasonal hunting
The fat from the marmot is considered medicinal — applied to skin and drunk
dinner.description: Mongolia's whole-animal cooking from the inside out — a marmot or young goat packed with incandescent stones, sealed, and blowtorched externally while the internal stones cook from within. Both sides cook simultaneously. One of the world's most ancient cooking techniques. The marmot's fat is considered medicinal in Mongolian folk medicine.

dinner.name: Aaruul (Dried Curd Snack)
ingredients: Aaruul — dried curds of fermented milk (no recipe to make in-home: it's an extended fermentation-drying process)
instructions: Aaruul is Mongolia's preserved dairy food — the nomad's trail food
Made from the curds of fermented milk, dried in the sun for weeks
The result: hard, white or yellow lumps of dried fermented milk
Very hard — Mongolians chip off pieces with their teeth
Very sour from the fermentation
High in protein and calories — sustained nomads on long horseback journeys
Aaruul keeps for months without refrigeration — essential in the steppe
Each family makes aaruul from their own animals' milk
The milk source varies by season: cow, mare, yak, goat
The taste is intensely sour and funky — aged cheese meets dried yogurt
This entry is listed as a snack/food item — the actual production is a multi-week process
dinner.description: Mongolia's trail food — sun-dried fermented milk curds, intensely sour and very hard. Chipped off and eaten in pieces. High in protein and calories, shelf-stable for months: the nomad's sustenance on long horseback journeys across the steppe. Each family makes their own aaruul from their own animals. The taste is intensely sour and funky — aged dairy in solid, dried form.

snacks.name: Boortsog (Fried Dough)
instructions: Mix dough, rest
Shape into various forms
Deep fry until golden
snacks.description: Fried dough — served at every Mongolian celebration and meal.

snacks.name: Ul Boov (Shoe Sole Cake)
ingredients: Layers: dried curd, candy, sugar pieces
instructions: Ul boov is the Mongolian Tsagaan Sar (Lunar New Year) cake-tower
A stack of fried dough circles (resembling shoe soles — hence the name)
Each cake is fried in oil until puffed and crispy
The cakes are stacked in specific odd numbers (3, 5, 7, or 9) — odd numbers only
Between layers: dried curds (aaruul), candy, sugar pieces
The height of the stack signals family status and good wishes for the year
Ul boov is not eaten during the celebration — it's a centerpiece and symbol
It's only disassembled at the end of the festival period
The shoe-sole shape comes from the resemblance to the sole of a Mongolian boot (traditional footwear)
The ul boov tower is the visual centerpiece of every Mongolian Tsagaan Sar celebration
snacks.description: Mongolia's Lunar New Year tower — fried dough circles stacked in odd numbers (3, 5, 7, or 9, with layers of dried curd and candy between, the height signaling family status) placed as the visual and symbolic centerpiece of Tsagaan Sar celebrations. Not eaten during the festival — it's a symbol. The shoe-sole shape (ul boov) references the sole of a traditional Mongolian boot.

snacks.name: Toirog (Deep Fried Dough)
ingredients: Flour, water, salt, baking powder (or yeast)
Animal fat or oil for frying
instructions: Mix flour, water, salt, baking powder into a soft dough
Rest briefly
Shape into round flat discs or strips
Fry in animal fat or oil — the animal fat gives more flavor than vegetable oil
They puff and brown — crispy outside, airy inside
Toirog is Mongolia's everyday fried bread — like the Navajo fry bread or Lakota fry bread in the Americas
The nomadic bread: no oven needed, just fat and fire
Made when camping on the steppe — a quick bread from minimal ingredients
Also made at home and sold at markets
The fried dough in animal fat is deeply satisfying in cold weather
snacks.description: Mongolia's nomadic fried bread — dough discs or strips fried in animal fat until puffed and golden. No oven required: fat and fire on the open steppe. Similar to Navajo fry bread (Americas) and Central Asian fried bread traditions — the convergent evolution of hot-fat-plus-dough-equals-bread across nomadic cultures worldwide.

snacks.name: Airag (Fermented Mare's Milk)
ingredients: Naturally occurring bacteria and yeast (traditional churning vessel)
instructions: Airag is Mongolia's national beverage — fermented mare's milk
The fermentation uses natural bacteria and yeast from the traditional leather container (khukhuur)
Fresh mare's milk is poured in and churned repeatedly for hours and days
The lactose ferments into lactic acid and a small amount of alcohol (1-3%)
The resulting airag is mildly alcoholic, fizzy, sour, slightly pungent
It is both food and drink — complete nutrition in liquid form
Mare's milk season: June-September when mares have foals
The milking of mares and the making of airag is a central Mongolian summer activity
Airag is offered at every ger — more immediately than süütei tsai in summer
UNESCO recognized airag-making as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Mongolia
snacks.description: Mongolia's fermented mare's milk — lactose fermented by natural bacteria and yeast into a mildly alcoholic (1-3%), fizzy, sour drink. Made only June-September when mares lactate. Complete liquid nutrition. Offered at every ger in summer; UNESCO-recognized Intangible Cultural Heritage. The churning process (thousands of strokes) and the specific bacteria in the traditional leather vessel are irreplaceable.

desserts.name: Ul Boov (Shoe Sole Cake)
instructions: Make firm dough
Shape into sole-like ovals with decorative stamps
Deep fry until golden
Stack in towers, fill with aaruul and sweets
desserts.description: Decorative fried cookies stacked into towers for celebrations.

desserts.name: Boortsog (Deep Fried Cookie)
instructions: Mix flour, eggs, sugar, butter, baking powder into a stiff dough
Roll and cut into various shapes — diamond, oval, twisted strips
Fry in fat until golden
They puff slightly — crispy and rich
Boortsog is Mongolia's traditional celebration cookie — made for Tsagaan Sar and Naadam
They're made in large quantities and placed in bowls for guests to take
The deep frying in animal fat is the traditional method
Modern versions use vegetable oil
The dough is slightly sweet — these are not intensely sweet desserts
The crunch and the fried fat flavor is the pleasure
Stacked in a bowl as an offering to guests: take freely, eat freely
desserts.description: Mongolia's celebration cookie — stiff dough cut into shapes and deep-fried until golden and crunchy, piled in bowls for guests at Tsagaan Sar and Naadam festival. Not intensely sweet — a mildly sweet, deeply fried, satisfying crunch. Made in large quantities and offered freely. The traditional frying in animal fat (tallow) gives a specific flavor.

desserts.name: Tarag (Fermented Milk Yogurt)
ingredients: Tarag culture (previous batch of tarag — a spoonful starters a new batch)
instructions: Heat milk to 45°C — the correct temperature for yogurt fermentation
Add a spoonful of tarag (previous batch) — this contains the live culture
Stir gently, cover and keep warm 6-8 hours
The milk sets into a tangy, thick yogurt
The tarag culture passes from batch to batch — families maintain cultures for generations
Mongolian tarag is tangier than commercial yogurt — the wild culture is more complex
Eaten plain, as a condiment with meat, or used in cooking
Tarag is the daily Mongolian dairy — made from whatever milk is available (cow, yak, goat, camel)
The culture adaptation to each animal's milk creates slightly different flavors
Yak tarag is the richest and most complex
desserts.description: Mongolia's daily fermented milk — yogurt made from whole milk and an heirloom culture passed through generations, each batch started by a spoonful of the last. Mongolian tarag uses wild cultures more complex than commercial yogurt bacteria. The same culture adapts to cow, yak, goat, and camel milk — each producing a slightly different flavor. Yak tarag is the richest.

drinks.name: Airag (Fermented Mare's Milk)
instructions: Add starter to mare's milk in leather bag
Churn or stir regularly
Ferment 2-3 days
Serve cold
drinks.description: Fermented mare's milk — Mongolia's ancient national drink.

drinks.name: Arkhi (Milk Vodka)
instructions: Distill fermented milk in copper still
Collect clear spirit
Serve at room temperature

drinks.name: Shimiin Arkhi (Milk Vodka)
ingredients: Aaruul or tarag (fermented dairy as the base)
instructions: Shimiin arkhi is Mongolia's traditional distilled spirit — milk vodka
Made by distilling fermented dairy (airag or tarag) in a simple copper pot still
The process: heat the fermented milk, collect the steam in a coil, condense it
The resulting liquid is a clear spirit — 10-15% alcohol
Much lower alcohol than grain vodka — milder
The flavor is dairy-based: slightly sweet, milky, smooth
Shimiin arkhi is made at home across rural Mongolia — every ger that keeps animals makes it
The distillation equipment is simple and traditional
Offered to guests at celebrations alongside airag and süütei tsai
Milk vodka is produced commercially in Mongolian markets now
One of the world's most unusual spirits — distilled from fermented dairy rather than grain or fruit
drinks.description: Mongolia's milk vodka — fermented dairy (airag or tarag) distilled in a simple copper still into a mild (10-15% alcohol), slightly sweet, dairy-flavored clear spirit. One of the world's most unusual spirits: distilled from dairy, not grain or fruit. Made in every rural Mongolian ger. Offered at celebrations alongside airag. Now commercially produced.
